Esta es, probablemente, la pregunta de á: This is probably the most repeated algebra question in the exam: “discuss the following system according to the values of the parameter $k$ and solve it when it is consistent and determinate”. It is frightening because there seem to be infinitely many cases, one for each value of $k$. In fact there are almost always only three, and there is a method for finding them that never fails.
Todo lo que hace falta está ya en el cur: Everything needed is already in the course: [[al-gauss|Gauss's method]], the [[al-determinantes|rank]] and [[al-determinantes|determinants]]. Here they come together in a theorem and a recipe.
$A$ es la matriz de coeficientes y $A^*$:
$A$ is the coefficient matrix and $A^*$ the augmented one, with the column of constant terms attached.

It reads: “if the rank of A and that of A augmented differ, the system is inconsistent; if they equal the number of unknowns, it is consistent and determinate; if they are equal but smaller, consistent and indeterminate”.

And in the indeterminate case, the number of degrees of freedom — how many unknowns are left free as parameters — is $n - \operatorname{rank}(A)$.
Por qué es cierto, sin demostración form: Why it is true, without a formal proof: the rank of $A$ counts how many equations are genuinely independent. If adding the column of results raises the rank, there is an equation that combines the others in its coefficients but not in its result: it says something like “$0 = 5$”. If it does not rise, there is no contradiction, and what remains to know is whether there are as many useful equations as unknowns.

Determinant and critical values. $\det A = \begin{vmatrix} k & 1 \\ 1 & k \end{vmatrix} = k^2 - 1$, which vanishes at $k = 1$ and $k = -1$.

Gabriel Cramer, un matemático suizo, pub: Gabriel Cramer, a Swiss mathematician, published his rule in 1750 in a book on algebraic curves: he wanted to know how many points are needed to determine a curve, and that led him to systems of equations. The rank theorem has a stranger history: in Spain it is called Rouché-Frobenius, in Italy Rouché-Capelli, in Russia Kronecker-Capelli and in France Rouché-Fontené. Several mathematicians stated it almost simultaneously around 1875 and each country kept its own.
Un sistema es <strong>homogéneo</strong>: A system is homogeneous when all its constant terms are zero. It can then never be inconsistent, because $x = y = z = 0$ is always a solution: the trivial solution. The only interesting question is whether it has others.
\\text{un sistema homogéneo cuadrado tie: \text{a square homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions} \iff \det A = 0
Se lee: <em>«tiene soluciones distintas:
It reads: “it has solutions other than the trivial one if and only if the determinant of A is zero”.

Because if $\det A \ne 0$ the system is consistent and determinate and its only solution is the trivial one; if $\det A = 0$ the rank drops, it is indeterminate and it has infinitely many.
Ajustar una reacción química es resolver: Balancing a chemical reaction is solving a homogeneous system. In $a\,\mathrm{CH_4} + b\,\mathrm{O_2} \to c\,\mathrm{CO_2} + d\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ each element gives an equation — carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms are all conserved — and all of them are set to zero. The trivial solution is of no use, so the system has to be indeterminate, and the simplest whole-number solution is the coefficients: 1, 2, 1, 2. Chemistry programs do exactly this. In economics, Leontief's tables, describing how much each sector needs from the others, are linear systems whose discussion says whether an economy can sustain itself.
